results.margin: Near-to-far gap is 12.1 ns against a 1.2 ns noise floor (~10x), and 1353 MB/s against 289 MB/s (~4.7x). results.consequence: Anything reading numa_distance() treats these four domains as interchangeable. Page placement and migration policy driven by the declared matrix systematically underestimates crossing cost.
results.note: Magnitudes differ 4x between metrics: latency spans 11% across pairs (18% counting local), bandwidth only 3.5% (4.9%). A bandwidth-only study would reasonably call these domains interchangeable. Which metric you measure determines whether you see the topology at all.

aggregate_observation.discriminator: Re-run pinned to a different domain. If 'fastest' follows the thread it is our artifact; if it stays node 0 it is a machine property and deserves its own claim.

That turns numa.distance_matrix from 'firmware tables are unreliable' into 'AMD describes its GPU interconnect accurately and its CPU interconnect not at all' -- specific and actionable rather than lazy.

results.secondary_defect: craype-hugepages2M provisions only the LOCAL node's pool. Once linked, the default allocator ABORTS under a remote `numactl -m`. conditions.note: -c 14 confines each rank to one NUMA domain; Cray MPICH refuses NIC_POLICY=NUMA otherwise. Placement verified per rank.

control.question: Does MPICH_OFI_NIC_POLICY=NUMA do the work, or does rank spread?
control.finding: The policy does essentially NOTHING. What matters is spreading ranks across NUMA domains; the default policy then assigns NICs correctly on its own. Without this arm we would have credited the policy for a 4x speedup it had no part in -- and put that in the briefing as advice.

results.margin: Scaling is linear to 4 pairs: 22.7 -> 45.1 -> 90.3 GB/s. The node reaches 90.3 GB/s, ~90% of the declared 100 GB/s. The July 23.9 GB/s was PER LINK and the spec is correct; only the natural single-pair benchmark misleads.
results.consequence: Quoting the single-pair result next to the 100 GB/s node spec looks like a 4x error. The declared number is correct; the natural benchmark configuration measures something else.

regimes.reason: PEAK. Working set still fits in L3 (32 MB per L3 region) but needs 8192 PTEs at 4K, far past TLB reach. Every access pays a page walk that itself goes to memory.
Both effects saturated; settles to a roughly constant offset

measured_under.access_pattern: dependent random (pointer chase) -- each load depends on the previous
measured_under.working_set: swept, 256 KB to 1 GB; the 2.4x is at 32 MB

not_measured: streaming / sequential access -- the regime where the mechanism does not apply. A corsys4 bandwidth check (107,765 huge vs 107,342 4K) suggests no effect, but that is a different machine and a bandwidth metric, so it does not settle the latency question here.
multi-threaded first touch across a 2 MB page boundary -- a 2 MB page can span data first-touched by threads on different NUMA domains, which coarsens placement
write or mixed traffic
under memory load from co-resident ranks
results.mechanism: The penalty comes from TLB reach failure on accesses that cannot be prefetched. 32 MB needs 8192 PTEs at 4 KB, far past the ~8 MB L2 TLB reach, so every access pays a page walk that itself misses to memory. It exists only where BOTH hold: the working set exceeds TLB reach, AND the access pattern defeats prefetch. A kernel that streams contiguously amortises the page walk across the whole page, so the mechanism is absent and no benefit should be expected.
results.margin: Zero, then 2.4x, then a constant offset. There is no single number that describes this.
results.consequence: TLB misses reported as memory latency. The worst case is at a working set that still fits in cache, which is exactly where a developer would not look for it.
results.note: MEASURED CONSEQUENCE OF USING THIS OUTSIDE ITS REGIME: an agent matched a streaming kernel's working set against the curve above -- correctly, per the regime variable declared at the time -- and enabled huge pages for it. It cost 2.7% (p=3e-10) rather than helping. The number did not merely fail to transfer; it inverted. That is why regime_variables is a list and why measured_under exists. Full write-up in eval/exp-b/RESULTS.md.

results.cross_validation: Idle floor 89.0 ns agrees with ptrchase huge-page local (85.9 ns) and the cache curve DRAM plateau (87.9 ns) -- three measurements, two independent tools, within 3.5%.
results.method_note: The original 19-point sweep placed both knee endpoints inside a single gap and rendered the entire transition as one vertical jump. Densifying across 48-96 is what made the operating point visible.

measured_under.regime_swept: injection delay, densified across 48-96 after the original 19-point sweep hid the knee
measured_under.node_state: idle apart from the load generator

not_measured: Read/write mix. This probe sweeps read-only traffic; MLC sweeps ratios. Write traffic saturates differently, and hwloc defines an empty WriteLatency slot waiting for it.
Whether the knee moves with page size or NUMA placement -- neither was varied.
results.mechanism: Latency rises steeply near saturation because queueing delay grows without bound as utilisation approaches 1, while delivered bandwidth is already asymptotically flat. The knee is where that queueing term starts to dominate. It is a property of the memory controllers under READ load; a different read/write mix moves it.
results.margin: 98.3% of peak bandwidth is available at 2.7x lower latency. Between injection delay 52 and 56 latency collapses 634 -> 234 ns while bandwidth falls only 1.7%.
results.consequence: Tuning to saturate bandwidth costs a factor of 2.7 in latency for 1.7% of throughput.
results.open: A 400 ns step remains between delay 52 and 56. The transition is genuinely sharp but has not been proven with points inside it.

results.control: GPU-aware MPI run with HOST buffers on both ends landed within 0.02% of plain host. Enabling GPU support costs nothing by itself; the entire 5.5% lives in the hardware path between the NIC and the memory it reads. One run eliminated a whole hypothesis family.

eliminated.how: advantage is FLAT at 5.5% from 64 to 1024 pages, a 16x range. A scatter-gather cost would grow with page count. Nine independent points say it does not.

results.working_account: A per-message CPU-side cost in the device path -- plausibly a fence or flush making GPU writes visible to the NIC -- explains the small-message penalty and the crossover. The residual steady-state 5.5% is not explained by amortisation alone; coherence on host DMA is the leading candidate.
results.practical: Bandwidth turns positive at 16 KB, latency not until 256 KB -- a streaming benchmark keeps messages in flight and amortises the fixed cost, a ping-pong pays it every round trip. Production GPU HPC and LLM training move megabytes and sit far above both crossovers. The small-message penalty applies to halo exchanges and small collectives.

measured_under.pattern: ping-pong (osu_latency) and streaming (osu_bw) reported separately -- the crossover differs between them, which is why both are recorded
measured_under.gcd_selection: NOT RECORDED at measurement time -- recovered from evidence files if at all
measured_under.memory_type: device-resident vs host-staged; pinned/pageable NOT RECORDED at measurement time -- recovered from evidence files if at all

not_measured: Intra-node device-to-device transfer -- this claim is inter-node only.
Under network load from other users, and the fabric is shared.
Whether the crossover moves with GCD choice or NUMA placement of the host buffer.
results.mechanism: Device buffers avoid a staging copy but pay a fixed per-transfer setup that host staging does not. Below the crossover the fixed cost dominates and staging wins; above it the avoided copy dominates and device wins. The crossover therefore sits wherever those two costs cross, which is why it differs between ping-pong and streaming: a streaming benchmark keeps messages in flight and amortises the fixed cost.
results.margin: The 4 MiB bandwidth gap is 82x the across-pass spread; the latency gap is 30x. Device latency varied 0.02 us across three passes (0.011%) -- the most reproducible measurement in the campaign. Passes were INTERLEAVED, not blocked, so drift over the allocation cannot masquerade as a residency effect.
results.open: Contention versus cache coherence on host DMA. The discriminating test was confounded -- see cost.contention_sensitivity.

results.confound: The load generator consumes cores as well as bandwidth. The GPU-direct path needs more host CPU, so core starvation swamped the effect under test. Recorded as confounded rather than reported as a number.

unplanned_finding.statement: GPU-direct is markedly more sensitive to CPU contention than host transfers -- 75% degradation versus 50%.
unplanned_finding.note: Nobody set out to measure this. It matters, because a real application is using its cores. It survives the confound because the confound IS the finding here.

results.next_step: Separate core pressure from bandwidth pressure -- pin the load generator off the ranks under test, or drive memory load from a different domain.

measured_under.status: CONFOUNDED -- probe_validated is no, confidence low. These conditions describe an attempt, not a measurement.
measured_under.load_generator: shared the cores under test rather than being pinned off them; that is the confound

not_measured: Everything. This claim has no usable value in any regime. It is retained because a characterization on an idle node describes a machine nobody runs on, and recording the failed attempt is more honest than an empty slot.
results.margin: The result INVERTS the idle-state gap, which is backwards for memory contention -- device transfers never touch the loaded DDR4.

Captures the four uncaptured declared sources, then measures a /proc/interrupts delta (where IRQs actually land vs where smp_affinity_list says) and per-core jitter (whether the reservation is sufficient at all). bin/jitter validated on corsys4: uniform jitter, no core above 2x the median -- correct for a box with no core specialization.

declared.implication: reads as ~252 G of node-local scratch disk available to any job

not_measured: Bandwidth of any tier -- this claim is inventory only. See cost.storage_bands.
Whether the NVMe is shared with other jobs on the same node.
Metadata rates on any tier.
results.mechanism: The NVMe device exists on every node but is only mapped into the job when the nvme constraint is requested. df therefore reports the tmpfs overlay in a default allocation, and a tmpfs size limit is not free storage: it is a ceiling on how much RAM the job may convert into apparent disk.
results.margin: 3.4 TB of local disk is invisible without one constraint flag, while 252 G of RAM is displayed as though it were disk.
results.consequence: A job writing bulk per-rank output to /tmp consumes node memory and dies out of memory, with the failure appearing to be in the application. A job that could have staged 3.4 TB locally instead writes it to a single Lustre stripe.

measured_under.ranks_per_node: 8, FIXED -- more ranks means more nodes, not different packing
measured_under.fabric_state: SHARED with all other users; occupancy recorded in the run conditions file. This claim varies with what other jobs are doing in a way that memory-side claims do not.

not_measured: Beyond 128 ranks / 16 nodes. Alltoall is already superlinear at 128 and the extrapolation is the interesting part, so this bound matters.
Ranks-per-node other than 8 -- on-node packing was deliberately held fixed, so nothing here separates rank scaling from per-node contention.
GPU-resident buffers.
Non-power-of-two rank counts, where Cray MPICH may select a different algorithm.
Under network load from the job itself, as opposed to from other users.
results.mechanism: Small-message collectives are bound by hop count and per-message overhead, so cost grows roughly with the depth of the reduction or broadcast tree -- logarithmic-ish in rank count. Large-message allreduce is bandwidth bound and each rank moves a nearly fixed volume regardless of how many peers exist, so it barely grows. Alltoall is different in kind: total messages grow as n^2, so per-rank time grows WITH the rank count and the growth is superlinear once messages are large enough to be bandwidth bound.
results.margin: Growth from 8 to 128 ranks spans 1.6x to 26.3x depending on operation and message size -- a factor of 16 difference in the scaling exponent itself.
results.consequence: A scaling study extrapolated from point-to-point numbers, or from one message size, predicts the wrong rank count to stop at. A code dominated by small allreduces and one dominated by large alltoall have opposite scaling behaviour on the same fabric.
results.note: THE FINDING IS THE DISAGREEMENT. The two regime axes do not have the same shape: allreduce at 1 MiB grows 1.6x over the same rank range where alltoall at 64 KiB grows 26.3x. So no scalar and no single curve describes collective cost here -- it is a surface, and any summary that collapses either axis is wrong somewhere. This was pre-registered as the falsifiable question and could have come out the other way: matching shapes would have meant one curve sufficed.

flagged.statement: Per-GCD HBM latency spans 365-397 ns, and pairs (0,3), (1,4), (2,5) match within 0.3 ns.

pitfalls.symptom: Latency measurements come out high with no error anywhere.
pitfalls.cause: THP is [never] and the hugetlb pool is empty (Total 4, Free 0). Both normal paths fail silently.
pitfalls.remedy: Load craype-hugepages2M -- it works by relinking, not a runtime flag. Then verify via smaps; do not trust the madvise return.
pitfalls.sting: Once linked, the default allocator ABORTS under a remote `numactl -m`, because the module provisions only the local node's pool. Local latency and the NUMA matrix need two separate passes.
pitfalls.provenance_note: THP setting and hugetlb pool are readable by anyone (/sys/kernel/mm/..., /proc/meminfo), and craype-hugepages2M is in the OLCF user guide. The '~16 ns high' figure was ours and is removed.

pitfalls.cause: One core per L3 group is OS-reserved: 0, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 56.
pitfalls.remedy: `-c 56` is the ceiling. It also divides cleanly: 14 cores / 28 threads per NUMA domain.
pitfalls.provenance_note: OLCF documents low-noise-mode core specialization; Cpus_allowed_list shows it to any process.

pitfalls.symptom: Topology conclusions drawn on a login node do not hold on compute.
pitfalls.cause: login08 is EPYC 7763 + a single MI210; compute is 7A53 + 4x MI250X.
pitfalls.remedy: Both are gfx90a so builds carry over, but no topology measurement from a login node is valid. Run 00_topo.sh inside an allocation.
pitfalls.provenance_note: Login and compute node specs are both published.

pitfalls.symptom: Inter-node bandwidth from one rank per node reads far below the node spec.
pitfalls.cause: One rank per node crosses one of four Slingshot NICs.
pitfalls.remedy: Spread ranks across the four NUMA domains -- `-c 14` gives one rank per domain.
pitfalls.provenance_note: Four NICs and the 100 GB/s figure are published. The 22.7/45.1/90.3 scaling was measured by us today and is removed from the declared rendering.

pitfalls.symptom: OSU 7.4 fails to build against the Cray toolchain.
pitfalls.cause: c/upc is unconditionally in the top-level SUBDIRS and there is no configure flag to disable it; the Cray compiler has no UPC front end.
pitfalls.provenance_note: We hit this building OSU. Not in any OLCF document.

pitfalls.symptom: The shipped Frontier build script fails or takes 4-8 hours.
pitfalls.cause: config/build_olcf_frontier_ROCm.sh hardcodes BOOST_ROOT to /ccs/proj/mat151 (inaccessible outside that project) and builds all eight variants.
pitfalls.remedy: Use the boost/1.86.0 module and build only gpu_real -- about 15 minutes.
pitfalls.provenance_note: We hit this building QMCPACK. Not in any OLCF document.

pitfalls.symptom: A CMake project builds cleanly under the default environment and runs single-threaded. The timer table looks normal; nothing errors.
pitfalls.cause: Frontier defaults to PrgEnv-cray. CCE identifies to CMake as "CrayClang", which matches a "Cray" branch BEFORE any "Clang" branch in projects that test in that order. If the project ships no CrayCompilers.cmake, it falls through to a warning and sets no flags at all -- including -fopenmp. Configuration.h then substitutes stub omp_* functions, so every `omp parallel for` and `omp simd` is silently dropped.
pitfalls.remedy: module load PrgEnv-gnu, and verify: grep ENABLE_OPENMP build/src/config.h must show 1. Do not trust a clean build.
pitfalls.sting: Observed on miniQMC 2026-08-13. The failure costs a factor of the thread count and presents as "this machine is slow", not as a build problem.

pitfalls.symptom: `srun -n16` completes, prints one timer table, and reports a plausible time. Scaling studies show no speedup and no error.
pitfalls.cause: Some CMake projects default MPI OFF (miniQMC: SET(QMC_MPI 0 ...)). Without it the binary is serial, so N ranks are N independent copies of the whole problem rather than one N-rank job. Nothing in the output says so unless the code happens to print MPI rank count.
pitfalls.remedy: Pass the project's MPI flag explicitly and verify HAVE_MPI in the generated config header. Prefer a benchmark that prints its rank count, and check it.
pitfalls.sting: Detected only because miniQMC prints "MPI processes = N". A code that does not print it would have produced a full scaling study of nonsense.

pitfalls.symptom: CMake configure fails on a Cray system with FindMPI unable to accept the CC wrapper as an MPI compiler.
pitfalls.cause: CMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME must be CrayLinuxEnvironment for FindMPI to recognise the Cray compiler wrappers.
pitfalls.remedy: -DCMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME=CrayLinuxEnvironment. Note this also implies cross-compiling, which skips MPI_DETERMINE_LIBRARY_VERSION -- projects that test the resulting variable then abort, and need it defined manually.
pitfalls.sting: Two failures from one cause, the second appearing only after the first is fixed.

pitfalls.symptom: `df -h /tmp` on a compute node reports ~252 G available, so it reads as a generous node-local scratch disk. A job that writes tens or hundreds of GB there dies out of memory, and the failure points at the application rather than at the write.
pitfalls.cause: /tmp, /dev/shm and /rootfs.rw are all tmpfs on Frontier compute nodes -- they are RAM. Every byte written counts against the node memory the job is using. The 252 G figure is a tmpfs size limit, not free storage. /var/tmp and /mnt/bb are overlay, and /mnt/bb is NOT writable by default despite every node advertising the `nvme` Slurm feature, VERIFIED 2026-08-18: `-C nvme` mounts /dev/mapper/nvme-bb, an xfs filesystem of 3.4 TB, at /mnt/bb/$USER and it is writable. Without that constraint the device is present but unmounted, so df shows only the tmpfs and a user reading df gets the wrong answer twice: /tmp looks like local disk and is RAM, while 3.4 TB of real local disk is invisible.
pitfalls.remedy: Write bulk output to $MEMBERWORK or $PROJWORK (Lustre), or request node-local NVMe with `#SBATCH -C nvme` and use /mnt/bb/$USER. Use /tmp only for small transient files and count them against the memory budget.
pitfalls.sting: Observed on frontier06028, 2026-08-18. $HOME is NFS and not Lustre either (lfs exits 25 there), so neither of the two paths a user reaches for by habit is the right one for bulk I/O.

Can measured distances be injected back via hwloc_distances_add, so existing consumers (MPI, Slurm, mpibind, ZeroSum) pick up corrected values with no code change? Unverified against the hwloc version on Frontier -- and if it works it is the strongest deployment path in the project.
Is the SLIT-vs-measured discrepancy already known to OLCF, or a known firmware simplification?
Read/write mix for loaded latency -- currently read-only.
Does the uniform node-0 host preference follow the probe's main thread? Re-run pinned to a different domain. If it does, it is our artifact; if not, it is a machine property with no declared source.

observations.statement: Host-memory latency splits by GCD die parity. Even dies (0,2,4,6) mean 1382 ns; odd dies (1,3,5,7) mean 1224 ns. The slowest odd die beats the fastest even one in every pass.

conditions.host_memory: explicitly bound per NUMA domain, verified with move_pages

observations.why_promoted: July flagged this and declined to claim it for one specific reason: host memory used default hipHostMalloc placement, so the NUMA domain was uncontrolled and the absolute numbers were 'to some host domain'. That caveat is gone -- every allocation is now bound and verified. And the separation holds in all three passes tested INDEPENDENTLY, which pooling would not have established: pooling lets one lucky pass carry a result.
observations.secondary_structure: Even dies are also NUMA-sensitive (across-domain range 88-175 ns) while odd dies are nearly flat (27-55 ns), and even dies are far noisier pass-to-pass (129-155 ns vs 29-43 ns).
observations.consequence: Host-memory-bound kernels should prefer odd GCDs; peer-heavy kernels the even ones. Nothing in ROCm's placement logic knows this, and no declared source reports it.
observations.remaining_caveat: One node type, one node. Not established machine-wide.

hmat.finding: hwloc 2.11.2 defines six memory-attribute slots for cost on this machine and the firmware fills none of them. The container for measured cost exists, is typed, is per-(initiator, target), and is empty. Filling it is additive -- hwloc-annotate can register custom named attributes alongside these.
hmat.pointed_detail: The Read/Write split is finer than our own data. Our loaded-latency sweep is read-only and 'write traffic saturates differently' is an open question we recorded in July. hwloc has a named empty slot waiting for exactly that number.
